name: ReasoningBank

paper.title: ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory

construction.unit: memory item: title, one-line description, 1-3 sentence content; up to 3 per finished task
construction.kept_as: LLM-distilled strategies and lessons (the raw trajectory is stored alongside but never read)
construction.processing: LLM judge labels the finished trajectory success/failure; a success prompt asks why it worked, a failure prompt asks what to avoid
construction.writer: the agent's own backbone LLM (Gemini-2.5-flash/pro or Claude-3.7-sonnet), temperature 1.0

organization.structure: flat list of per-task entries (query, trajectory, label, memory items)
organization.stores: one JSONL bank plus one query-embedding cache per website subset (code)
organization.index: gemini-embedding-001 (3072-d) embedding of each past task query

management.operations: append the new entry after every task; no merging, pruning or rewriting

retrieval.query: the new task's query, prefixed with an instruction to find helpful prior queries (code)
retrieval.candidates: cosine similarity between the new query and every past task query
retrieval.selection: top-k past tasks, k = 1 by default; all their memory items are returned
retrieval.budget: 1 past task, i.e. up to 3 items (up to 5 after MaTTS parallel extraction)

use.context: memory items appended to the agent's system prompt with a note to decide at each step whether to use each item
use.reasoning: ReAct web agent in BrowserGym, up to 30 steps; bash-only mini-SWE-agent for SWE-Bench

classify.note: Items are fetched as a block by similarity of task queries (top-1 task); the item text itself is never searched.

stages.ingestion: After each test task the agent's trajectory (think/action steps; code uses the agent's thinking as a stand-in for page observations) and final answer are collected; no ground truth is used.
stages.construction: The backbone LLM, prompted as a judge (temperature 0), labels the trajectory success or failure; a success-specific or failure-specific prompt then distils at most 3 memory items (title, description, content) at temperature 1.0.
stages.organization: Each task becomes one entry (query, trajectory, label, items) appended to a flat JSON bank; the query's embedding is cached separately. The code keeps one bank per WebArena website subset.
stages.update: Plain append after every task, including failures; no merging, pruning or deduplication. MaTTS instead extracts up to 5 items by contrasting k rollouts of the same task (parallel) or uses self-refinement notes (sequential).
stages.retrieval: The new query is embedded (gemini-embedding-001) and compared by cosine with past task queries; the memory items of the top-1 most similar past task are returned.
stages.answer: The items are appended to the agent's system prompt with an instruction to state at each step whether it uses each item; the ReAct agent then acts for up to 30 steps.

summary: Distils each finished agent task, judged by the agent itself as success or failure, into up to three short strategy or lesson items, retrieves the items of the most similar past task by query embedding, and adds memory-aware test-time scaling (MaTTS) that contrasts several rollouts of one task to write better items.

open_questions: Because retrieval compares task queries, the gain may come from reusing advice written for a near-duplicate task (WebArena tasks share templates) rather than from general strategies; the paper does not split results by template overlap.
The +MaTTS rows use 5 rollouts per task against 1 for the baselines; Fig. 5 shows memory-free scaling gains less, but compute is not matched in Table 1.

discussion.takeaway: Storing short, self-judged lessons from both successful and failed runs, instead of raw trajectories or success-only workflows, gives a web or coding agent a few points more success with fewer steps, and extra rollouts per task help more when they feed this memory.

claims.claim: Beats memory-free and trajectory/workflow memory on every backbone.
claims.evidence: WebArena overall SR +8.3 / +7.2 / +4.6 over No Memory for Gemini-2.5-flash / -pro / Claude-3.7 (48.8, 53.9, 46.3). Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Also helps on Mind2Web and SWE-Bench-Verified.
claims.evidence: Mind2Web cross-domain step SR 36.6 vs 31.9 (flash); SWE-Bench-Verified resolve rate 38.8 vs 34.2 (flash), 57.4 vs 54.0 (pro). Tables 2-3
WebArena-Shopping 46.5 with successes only, 49.7 with failures; AWM drops 44.4 → 42.2 when failures are added. Fig. 7, §5
At k = 5 parallel MaTTS 55.1 vs 52.4 for vanilla TTS and 42.2 without memory (Best-of-N, Shopping). Fig. 4, §4.3

claims.claim: Cheaper per task despite the extra LLM calls.
claims.evidence: 53.1k vs 50.8k tokens per task (+4.3%) for +20.5% relative SR; fewer steps, most on solved tasks (up to 2.1). Table 5, Table 4

limits: Only memory content is studied; episodic or hierarchical memory designs are not compared.
Retrieval (embedding similarity) and consolidation (append) are deliberately simple.
Success and failure labels come from an LLM judge and can be wrong on ambiguous tasks.
reading: The key used for lookup is the past task's query, not the stored strategy text, so the method retrieves by task similarity exactly like the trajectory baseline Synapse; only what is shown differs (App. B.1 says all methods share retrieval and consolidation).
More retrieved tasks hurt: k = 1 gives 49.7 on Shopping and k = 4 gives 44.4 (Fig. 13), so each prompt carries at most three items.
Memory is written from the test stream itself with self-judged labels; the code runs tasks in task-id order and keeps a separate bank for each WebArena site, including the 29-task Multi subset.
The judge agreed with gold labels 72.7% of the time; Fig. 8 simulates noisier and cleaner labels and reports small changes, with gold labels best.
+MaTTS rows in Table 1 use 5 rollouts per task and Best-of-N selection in Fig. 4; baselines use one rollout.
The released code covers WebArena and SWE-Bench only; the MaTTS scripts read a single trial folder, so the parallel self-contrast numbers cannot be reproduced from them as released.

abstract.text: ReasoningBank is a memory for LLM agents that face a stream of tasks and have no ground truth at test time. After each task the agent judges its own run, and an LLM distils short, reusable strategies from successes and cautionary lessons from failures; for a new task, the lessons of the most similar past task are placed in the prompt. The authors also propose memory-aware test-time scaling (MaTTS), which spends extra rollouts on each task and contrasts them to write better memory. On WebArena, Mind2Web and SWE-Bench-Verified it beats memory-free agents and trajectory or workflow memories in success rate and step count.
